plan.topic: Backed up in the days after a big holiday dinner on tirzepatide: how often the label reports constipation vs placebo, and gentle next-day habits
plan.angle: Title: 'Tirzepatide (Zepbound/Mounjaro) and Constipation: What the Label Says #shorts'. Sentence 1: 'Tirzepatide and feeling backed up over the holidays? Constipation is on the label.' Stat card: constipation was about 11 to 17% on Zepbound vs 5% on placebo over 72 weeks, with the population copied exactly from the Table 2 heading. Next, as its own label line with no 'so': tirzepatide delays gastric emptying. Two tips: sip fluids through the day unless you've been told to limit fluids, and take a gentle walk. Ask a pharmacist before any laxative. Then the Medication Guide red flag word for word, the fixed don't-stop line, 'Not personal advice, so ask your prescriber.' and the loop line.

plan.why: Holiday felt-symptom Shorts work (491, 320 and 263 views), and this morning-after GI moment hasn't been used in this year's holiday set. It feeds the Thanksgiving long video. | fact-check: A useful topic, but the label facts in the brief are off and the title invents a cause. (1) Table 2 in the current Zepbound label (DailyMed, revised 16 Nov 2026) gives constipation at week 72 as 17% (5 mg), 14% (10 mg) and 11% (15 mg) vs 5% for placebo, not 6%. 'Top dose vs placebo' (11% vs 5%) also picks the lowest rate. Give the range instead, with no dose numbers: 'about 11 to 17% vs 5% on placebo'. (2) The table pools Studies 1 and 2, and Study 2 enrolled adults with type 2 diabetes. Copy the population exactly as the table's heading states it, not the obesity-only wording in the brief. Cite the edition actually used with its real revision date (the 28 Aug 2026 date in our notes looks out of date). (3) The label doesn't tie constipation to big meals or holidays. The title and hook 'Backed up after the holiday dinner?' imply that the dinner causes it, which is the same cause-and-timing fault flagged on S3 11-23. Make the holiday the setting, not the cause. (4) The gastric emptying sentence must stand alone, with no 'so' and no link to constipation. (5) The red flag must copy the Medication Guide's patient wording: severe pain in your stomach area (abdomen) that will not go away, with or without vomiting → stop using it and call your healthcare provider right away. Name no laxative products, and keep 'unless you've been told to limit fluids'.

package.title: Tirzepatide (Zepbound): Backed Up This Holiday Season? What the Label Says #shorts
package.description:
Tirzepatide's label reports constipation in 11–17% of adults on tirzepatide (5, 10 or 15 mg) vs 5% on placebo over 72 weeks, in adults with obesity, or overweight plus a weight-related condition. What may help: sipping fluids through the day, unless you've been told to limit fluids, and a gentle walk. Ask a pharmacist before any laxative.
If you have severe pain in your stomach area (abdomen) that will not go away, with or without vomiting, stop using tirzepatide and call your healthcare provider right away. For anything that isn't that emergency sign, don't stop or change your medicine on your own.
#Tirzepatide
Not personal advice. Talk to your doctor or prescriber about whether it's right for you.

script.hook_pattern: myth-flip: sentence 1 puts the holiday first as the setting and then states the common belief ("This holiday season, people say feeling backed up on tirzepatide is just you."). Sentence 2 flips it with the label ("The label disagrees."). The holiday sits at the front of the sentence, away from the label line, so it is never read as the cause or as something the label says. The label number, with its comparator, population scope and timeframe, is spoken at about 5–6 s.

factcheck.summary:
This Short passes. Every claim matches its source, and the two issues I found are small on-screen wording fixes.

The constipation numbers in s2 match the Zepbound label (DailyMed, revised 16 November 2026), section 6.1, Table 1. That table pools Studies 1 and 2 and covers up to 72 weeks: 17% at 5 mg, 14% at 10 mg and 11% at 15 mg, against 5% on placebo. The population is adults with obesity or overweight, with or without type 2 diabetes, so the card's wording is accurate. Because the card doesn't say "without diabetes", it doesn't misstate who was in the trials.

The pancreatitis warning in s6 is copied word for word from the Medication Guide: "severe pain in your stomach area (abdomen) that will not go away, with or without vomiting", then stop and call your healthcare provider right away. I confirmed this sentence in Lilly's Medication Guide PDF, because the DailyMed page wouldn't show me the guide text.

The tips in s4 and s5 match the NHS constipation page (last reviewed 26 October 2023): drink plenty of fluids, take a daily walk, and speak to a pharmacist, who can suggest a suitable laxative. They're framed as "what may help", and the fluid tip keeps "unless you've been told to limit fluids".

The safety lines in s7 and s8 use the fixed single-sign wording. The word count checks out at 119, inside the tight arm of 90–120. The title stays within the label and names Zepbound. The holiday opener is set in the deliberately seasonal holiday slot, and it isn't presented as a cause.
